questions.question: In a 2D discrete Fourier transform (DFT) of an image, what does a point near the origin of the frequency domain primarily represent?
questions.choice_A: Low spatial frequency content corresponding to broad, slowly varying image structures
questions.choice_B: High spatial frequency content corresponding to fine edges and details
questions.choice_C: Phase information only, independent of magnitude
questions.choice_D: Artifacts introduced by the FFT implementation

questions.question: Which statement best captures the core finding from classic reconstruction experiments that swap magnitude and phase between two images?
questions.choice_A: Magnitude alone determines the recognizable content of an image
questions.choice_B: Phase largely preserves the structural and semantic layout, even when magnitude comes from another image
questions.choice_C: Swapping magnitude and phase produces identical reconstructions
questions.choice_D: Phase can be discarded without affecting image recognizability

questions.question: What is the most informative interpretation of the phase spectrum in a 2D DFT when reasoning about image structure?
questions.choice_A: It encodes the total energy at each frequency
questions.choice_B: It specifies the anisotropy of the power spectrum
questions.choice_C: It determines how different frequency components align in space to produce edges and contours
questions.choice_D: It removes the need for spatial domain representation

questions.question: Why are magnitude spectra of natural images commonly displayed with a logarithmic scale?
questions.choice_A: To linearize the phase
questions.choice_B: To reduce quantization errors in the FFT
questions.choice_C: Because the DC component is always zero otherwise
questions.choice_D: Because energy is heavily concentrated at low frequencies and spans several orders of magnitude

questions.question: When an image is translated by $(x_0, y_0)$ pixels, how does its 2D DFT change?
questions.choice_A: The magnitude stays the same while the phase is shifted by a linear ramp proportional to $(x_0, y_0)$
questions.choice_B: Both magnitude and phase are invariant to translation
questions.choice_C: Only the DC component changes, all other coefficients are unchanged
questions.choice_D: The spectrum rotates by an angle proportional to $(x_0, y_0)$

questions.question: What does the DC component (at frequency $(0,0)$) in the 2D DFT represent for an image?
questions.choice_A: The sharpest edges
questions.choice_B: The average intensity (mean) of the image
questions.choice_C: The strongest oriented features
questions.choice_D: An artifact that should always be removed

questions.question: Why can preserving phase while randomizing magnitude still yield a recognizable image?
questions.choice_A: Because magnitude carries only noise in natural images
questions.choice_B: Because phase encodes the histogram of pixel intensities
questions.choice_C: Because consistent phase alignment across frequencies anchors edges, shapes, and object boundaries
questions.choice_D: Because magnitude is primarily redundant across frequencies

questions.question: Which analogy between neural representations and Fourier phase is most appropriate?
questions.choice_A: Neuron firing rates correspond exactly to Fourier magnitude, making phase unnecessary
questions.choice_B: Neural population codes use only scalar magnitudes, whereas phase is a single neuron’s property
questions.choice_C: Fourier magnitude corresponds to preferred orientations, and phase corresponds to spatial frequency
questions.choice_D: Angular/directional coding in populations (e.g., orientation columns, head-direction cells) is analogous to phase specifying relative alignment and position

questions.question: What is a practical reason to center the zero frequency using an FFT-shift when visualizing 2D spectra?
questions.choice_A: It places low frequencies in the center, making radial and angular patterns easier to interpret
questions.choice_B: It eliminates negative frequencies from the spectrum
questions.choice_C: It converts complex values into real ones for display
questions.choice_D: It ensures aliasing cannot occur

questions.question: In natural image statistics, which magnitude-spectrum property is often observed?
questions.choice_A: Uniform power across all spatial frequencies
questions.choice_B: Approximately power-law decay with frequency (often described as 1/f behavior)
questions.choice_C: Power concentrated only at cardinal orientations
questions.choice_D: Power dominated by phase discontinuities

questions.question: In the 2D DFT, what does separability imply for transforming an image?
questions.choice_A: The transform must be computed globally, not by rows or columns
questions.choice_B: It cannot be implemented efficiently with FFT algorithms
questions.choice_C: The 2D DFT can be computed by applying 1D DFTs first along rows and then along columns (or vice versa)
questions.choice_D: Only square images can be transformed

questions.question: What is a key limitation of equating Fourier phase with all forms of “semantic” information in neural systems?
questions.choice_A: Phase is invariant to occlusion in all cases
questions.choice_B: Magnitude contains only sensor noise, not structure
questions.choice_C: Neural codes can be nonlinear, distributed, and task-dependent, so their “phase-like” aspects may not map cleanly onto Fourier phase
questions.choice_D: Fourier phase cannot represent edges

questions.question: Which scenario best illustrates that magnitude still conveys useful information despite the dominance of phase for recognizability?
questions.choice_A: Texture classification leveraging power spectrum statistics such as orientation energy distributions
questions.choice_B: Object localization using only phase congruency
questions.choice_C: Image alignment based solely on phase correlation
questions.choice_D: Phase-only holography

questions.question: In phase-based feature detection, what does “phase congruency” refer to?
questions.choice_A: Local maxima in magnitude across scales
questions.choice_B: Alignment of phase across multiple scales and orientations, indicating perceptually significant features like edges
questions.choice_C: The alignment of magnitudes across different images
questions.choice_D: The cancellation of phase near the DC component

questions.question: What visual artifact can arise when reconstructing an image from a subset of its Fourier coefficients without proper handling of boundaries?
questions.choice_A: Uniform gray-level shift
questions.choice_B: Rotation of the entire image
questions.choice_C: Gibbs-like ringing near sharp edges due to truncation/windowing
questions.choice_D: Loss of mean intensity only

questions.question: Which statement about randomizing phase while preserving magnitude is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: It preserves edge locations but alters textures
questions.choice_B: It often produces noise-like images that maintain global power spectrum statistics but lose coherent structure
questions.choice_C: It leaves the image visually unchanged
questions.choice_D: It only affects the DC component

questions.question: How does the convolution theorem inform our intuition about structure in images?
questions.choice_A: Convolution in the spatial domain corresponds to element-wise division in the frequency domain
questions.choice_B: Convolution in the spatial domain corresponds to element-wise multiplication of magnitudes only
questions.choice_C: Convolution in the spatial domain corresponds to multiplication in the frequency domain, where both magnitude and phase interact
questions.choice_D: Convolution in the frequency domain corresponds to addition in the spatial domain

questions.question: What is an important caveat when drawing analogies between Fourier phase and angular coding in neurons (e.g., head-direction cells)?
questions.choice_A: Neural tuning curves can be broad, noisy, and context-dependent, so the mapping from phase to direction may be at best qualitative
questions.choice_B: Neurons do not encode any directional information
questions.choice_C: Fourier phase is always uniform across frequencies, but neural tuning is not
questions.choice_D: Directional coding neurons only encode magnitude, not phase-like variables

questions.question: Why is phase unwrapping sometimes necessary when analyzing phase maps from the 2D DFT?
questions.choice_A: Because phase is stored as integer values that must be converted to floats
questions.choice_B: Because the magnitude depends on the unwrapped phase
questions.choice_C: Because phase is inherently modulo $2\pi$, causing discontinuities that can obscure smooth spatial variation
questions.choice_D: Because unwrapping reduces the DC component to zero

questions.question: Which practical observation bridges Fourier intuition with neural network feature maps in vision models?
questions.choice_A: Early convolutional layers often behave like random phase generators
questions.choice_B: Orientation- and position-sensitive units act somewhat like phase-sensitive components, while pooled energy statistics resemble magnitude
questions.choice_C: Deep networks discard low frequencies entirely
questions.choice_D: Neural networks encode only phase and no magnitude-like quantities
